newsitem.title: HONG KONG: E.Asian growth pause not a worrying trend - forum.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian growth pause not a worrying trend - forum.

text.p: The recent slowdown in East Asia's economic growth represents a pause, not a worrisome new trend, a panel of experts told delegates to the World Economic Forum meeting on Tuesday.
"The Asian miracle may be a thing of the past, but that doesn't mean that it is the end of high growth," said Toru Kusukawa, chairman of Fuji Research Institute Corp in Japan.

"At about 7.5 percent, growth in the region is still high and I think we will keep up that sort of growth for the rest of the decade," he said during a group discussion at the three-day annual forum focusing on East Asia-European relations.

East Asian economies have slowed recently as a result of deliberate policies to cool them, a worldwide slump in demand for Asia's electronics exports and a stronger dollar. But these factors were not enough to derail the region from its high growth track, said Manu Bhaskaran, director of Crosby Securities in Singapore.

Supply-side factors would continue to buoy growth, he said, citing good productivity, efficiency gains through privatisations, investments in infrastructure, trade liberalisation and strong foreign direct investment flows as areas which were helping underpin the region's economic strength.
While he expected growth to remain strong, Bhaskaran warned that the dynamic of growth has changed.
Governments could no longer rely on undervalued exchange rates and cheap labour to drive growth, he said.
"The structure of competition has changed, meaning that labour-intensive industries must be downsized, which brings pain," Bhaskaran said.
He said that while "superlative growth rates are assured, identifying losers and winners will be more difficult."
Guatam Kaji, managing director of the World Bank, was cautious in his outlook for East Asia, saying, "Getting the fundamentals right is necessary but not sufficient."
He said structural problems must be addressed if East Asia was to enjoy high growth levels in the longer term.

Driving infrastructure development through the greater participation of the private sector, reforming state enterprises, improving the financial sector by developing regulatory frameworks and assuring a strong banking system, and creating a skilled and mobile labour supply are necessary for Asia's healthy economic future, he said.
Policy makers also must pay more attention to preserving the environment and planning for increased energy needs into the next century, he said.
